title: Mental Biases
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/0/body: **Confirmation bias** means your mind only looks for evidence that backs up what you already think and ignores the rest. When you're long on a coin, you subconsciously notice only **bullish news and analysis**.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/1/body: For example, you only follow channels that agree with you, you don't see the **support that just broke**, or when your first reason turns out wrong, you find a fresh reason to stay in. The result is always the same: **admitting your mistake too late**, and a bigger loss.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: You're long on Bitcoin. The price has broken a key support, but you're scrolling social media for posts saying "it's just a fakeout." What is this behavior?
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/2/explana: You're only looking for evidence that confirms your earlier view and ignoring the support break, which says the opposite.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/3/prompt: Your analysis is bullish and you saw some good news too. But what does the 4-hour chart itself say?
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/3/explana: Every high and every low is lower than the one before. Read the chart as it is, not as you'd like it to be.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/4/title: The antidote: look for the opposite case
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/4/body: Before you enter, ask yourself **"What would prove me wrong?"** and write down the answer. That point is your analysis's **invalidation point**, and it's usually the sensible spot for your **stop loss** too.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: Add a "reasons against" column to your journal and write at least one before every trade.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/5/stateme: If every channel you follow agrees with your analysis, your analysis must be right.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/5/explana: Maybe you only follow channels that think like you do. Others agreeing doesn't make your analysis right; only price gets the final say.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/6/prompt: Which question before entering helps the most against confirmation bias?
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/6/options: What would prove my analysis wrong?
How many others took this trade?
What will I do with the profit?
Which channel agrees with my analysis?
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/6/explana: This question forces your mind to look for opposing evidence too, and to set your invalidation point in advance.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/7/sentenc: Before you enter, set your analysis's ___: the point where, if the price gets there, you accept you were ___.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/7/explana: Set your invalidation point while your mind is calm. That way, mid-trade, your bias can't make excuses for you.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/8/stateme: Changing your reason for a trade after your first reason turned out wrong is a sign of confirmation bias.
lessons/psychology-u2-l1/steps/8/explana: When the main reason you entered is gone, the trade should be closed. Finding a new reason to stay means your mind is defending its earlier view.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/0/body: Psychology research shows that the pain of a loss is usually **about twice** as strong as the joy of a gain of the same size. That's why your mind will do anything to avoid **locking in** a loss, even if it ends in a bigger one.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/1/body: Loss aversion leads to a dangerous pattern: you **close winners early** because you're scared they'll turn around, and you **hold losers** hoping they'll come back. That way, you can lose money overall even with a high win rate.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/2/prompt: You went long at the "Entry" line, and the price is getting close to your stop loss. Which thought comes from loss aversion?
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/2/options: "I'll move my stop a bit lower; it'll come back"
"If my stop gets hit, I'll accept it, per my plan"
"Once it closes, I'll log it in my journal"
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/2/explana: Moving your stop further away is running from accepting the loss. That one small move turns a 30-pip loss into a 100-pip loss.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/3/stateme: When your trade is in a loss, buying more at a lower price (averaging down) without a plan made in advance is a good way to escape the loss.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/3/explana: Adding to a losing position without a plan makes your risk bigger. It usually comes from hoping for a turnaround, not from analysis.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/4/body: Set your stop loss **before you enter**, with a calm mind, and afterward only move it in the direction that **lowers your risk**; never further away. Small losses are the normal cost of trading; **big losses are made from small losses you held on to.**
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/4/tip: If you can't accept a loss, your size is too big for your mind. Make it smaller.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/5/prompt: You have two open trades: one is $40 in profit and the other is $40 in loss. What does loss aversion usually tempt you to do?
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/5/options: Close the winner and keep the loser
Close the loser and keep the winner
Manage both exactly by the plan
Leave both open until take profit
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/5/explana: Your mind wants to "lock in" the profit and avoid "locking in" the loss. The result: small wins and big losses. Each trade's decision should come from your plan, not from the color of its number.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/6/sentenc: Loss aversion makes you close your ___ too early and hold your ___ too long.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/6/explana: Fear of a winner turning around gets you out early, and hope for a comeback keeps you stuck in losers.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/7/stateme: Moving your stop loss in the direction that lowers your risk doesn't go against discipline; the problem is moving it further away.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/7/explana: Tightening your stop (for example, to your entry after a good move) lowers your risk. Widening it means accepting a bigger loss than you planned.
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/8/pairs/0: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/8/pairs/1: Seeing only the evidence that agrees
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/8/pairs/2: Buying more while you're in a loss
lessons/psychology-u2-l2/steps/8/pairs/3: The point where your analysis is proven wrong
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/0/body: After a few wins in a row, you feel like you've **figured out the market**. Your mind takes your last few results too seriously (**recency bias**), even though a few wins in a row can be completely **random**.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/1/body: **Increasing your size**, breaking your rules ("I'm sure about this one") and entering without a setup. One loss at several times your normal size can wipe out the profit from several wins at once.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/2/prompt: You just had 3 wins in a row and feel like you're on a hot streak. You spot a half-formed setup that doesn't match your rules. What do you do?
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/2/options: Skip it, because it doesn't match your rules
Take it, because you're on a roll
Take it and double your size
Take it, but without a stop loss
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/2/explana: Your rules after a win are the same rules. A "hot hand" isn't a reason to enter; a valid setup is.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/3/stateme: 5 wins in a row prove your system has a high win rate.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/3/explana: 5 trades is a tiny sample; even a coin can land heads 5 times in a row. To judge a system, you need dozens or hundreds of trades.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/4/title: You have rules after a win too
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/4/body: **Keep your risk per trade fixed** (say, always 1% of your account) and only change it according to a plan written in advance, not a feeling. Many traders take a break after a really good day, **just like after a bad day**.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/4/tip: The feeling "this one's a sure thing" is a warning sign, not a signal.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/5/sentenc: After a winning streak, keep the ___ per trade fixed, and only enter when your plan's ___ are all met.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/5/explana: Fixed risk and clear entry conditions are your two main brakes against false confidence.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/6/prompt: Your account was $2,000 and you always risk 1%. After 4 wins, it's $2,160. By the 1% rule, what's the risk on your next trade?
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/6/explana: 1% × 2,160 = $21.60. Your risk grows slowly and automatically as your account grows, not suddenly several times over because you feel good.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/7/stateme: After a very profitable day, taking a break can be just as useful as after a losing day.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/7/explana: The thrill of winning clouds your judgment just like the frustration of losing. Stepping away helps you come back with a neutral mind.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/8/prompt: After 4 wins, you opened a long at double size. Now it's in a loss, you're only reading positive news, and you've moved your stop lower. Which biases are at work together?
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/8/options: Overconfidence, confirmation bias and loss aversion
Only FOMO; the rest is normal
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/8/explana: The double size came from overconfidence, reading only agreeing news is confirmation bias, and moving the stop further away is loss aversion. Biases usually come in chains.
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/9/pairs/1: Giving too much weight to your last few results
lessons/psychology-u2-l3/steps/9/pairs/3: The same risk percentage on every trade
